tldr: This paper presents EgoPHI, a vision model that simultaneously estimates dense contact regions and 3D contact force distributions across both hand and object mesh surfaces from a single monocular egocentric RGB image and an object 3D model. By generating dense force annotations using a physics simulator and validating with real-world optical sensing, the authors demonstrate practical 3D force estimation without wearable tactile sensors.
hero_caption: Overall concept of EgoPHI. Given a single monocular egocentric RGB image and an object template mesh as input, the model aligns the relative 3D pose of the hands and object, and directly estimates dense contact regions and 3D force vectors across both mesh vertices.
overview:
Understanding how humans dexterously manipulate objects from an egocentric (wearable camera) perspective is crucial for robots learning to imitate human tasks and collaborating safely. Prior work has made progress in detecting "where contact occurs" (contact regions) from images. However, knowing the contact location does not reveal "in which direction and with how much force" the person is pushing (contact forces). Yet dynamic force information is indispensable for assessing manipulation stability and human intent.

Inferring contact forces from monocular camera footage is extraordinarily hard. Heavy occlusions by the hands occur frequently, visual cues like subtle skin deformation or color changes are faint, and monocular images suffer from depth ambiguities along the 3D viewing direction. On top of that, the biggest bottleneck was the lack of large-scale datasets measuring the "ground-truth 3D forces across every mesh vertex" during complex hand-object interactions.

To solve this, the authors built a training pipeline that runs a physics simulator (SOFA) over existing hand-object interaction datasets to synthesize contact forces at each mesh vertex. They then developed EgoPHI, a deep learning model that leverages graph structures and cross-attention to capture hand-object geometric relationships, jointly refining the object's 3D pose while estimating dense contact and forces.

In evaluations on standard benchmarks (ARCTIC and H2O), EgoPHI outperformed existing baselines and achieved an average force error reduction of around 2 N on unseen objects. Furthermore, the team built custom physical sensing objects (a cuboid and a cylinder) based on frustrated total internal reflection (FTIR) and collected real-world data from eight participants. They demonstrated for the first time that a model trained purely on simulation transfers successfully to real-world 3D non-planar objects without collapsing (achieving sim-to-real transfer).
contributions: Proposed EgoPHI, the first vision model to estimate dense contact and 3D force distributions on both the interacting hands and the manipulated object's 3D mesh from a single monocular egocentric RGB image and object geometry.
Established a scalable data generation pipeline using a physics simulator to augment existing hand-object datasets with per-vertex contact force ground truth.

Fabricated optical tactile sensing objects (cuboid and cylinder) using frustrated total internal reflection, built a real-world contact force benchmark from eight participants across diverse touches and grasps, and demonstrated sim-to-real transfer.

sections.heading: From "Where is it touching?" to "How hard is it pushing?"
sections.summary: While human manipulation inherently relies on physical forces, estimating 3D forces from monocular egocentric video has been extremely difficult due to scarce visual cues and occlusions. This paper proposes EgoPHI to estimate dense contact and 3D forces across both hand and object meshes, demonstrating its effectiveness through simulated data and real-world experiments.
sections.details:
For robots to learn tasks by observing human demonstrations or to physically collaborate with people, they must understand not just where hands touch an object, but also how much force is applied. Recent computer vision models can localize hand-object contacts accurately, but capturing physical forces has remained out of reach.

Inferring forces from egocentric (wearable camera) RGB frames is far from straightforward. The hands frequently occlude large portions of the object, visual signs like skin blanching (whitening under pressure) are faint, and monocular images struggle with 3D directional depth ambiguities. Consequently, previous works were largely confined to 2D pressure heatmaps in image space or flat tabletop setups.

EgoPHI addresses this by taking a single monocular RGB image and an object template mesh to directly predict 3D forces and contact probabilities across the entire surface (every vertex) of both the hand and object meshes. The authors bypass the data shortage by synthesizing dense forces with a physics simulator, and they experimentally validate generalization to real environments using custom-built sensing objects.

sections.heading: Moving from contact to force, and from flat planes to 3D objects
sections.summary: While vision-based contact estimation across human bodies and hands has been actively explored, force estimation has remained confined to 2D image space or flat surfaces. EgoPHI builds on mesh representations from contact estimation and breaks new ground by extending vision-based force estimation to 3D articulated, non-planar objects.
sections.details:
Prior literature falls broadly into two streams:

### Vision-Based Contact Region Estimation
These techniques detect contact regions over full-body meshes (like SMPL) or hand meshes (MANO). Hand-object contact involves a dual imbalance problem: most vertices are not in contact (class imbalance), and contacts heavily concentrate on fingertips (spatial imbalance). Modern approaches such as HACO tackle this with specialized sampling and loss designs, but they only classify contact occurrence and cannot predict force magnitudes or directions.

### Vision-Based Force Estimation
Other works infer external forces inversely from object motions in video, observe tissue deformations in robotic surgery, or estimate grasp forces from robot hand cameras. In human hand-object interaction, representative works like PressureVision and EgoPressure emerged recently. However, PressureVision predicts 2D heatmaps in image space, and EgoPressure only estimates forces when hands press flat tables. Until now, no vision model could estimate forces on the 3D surface of volumetric objects during grasping and manipulation.

sections.heading: Physics-simulated force generation and a three-stage interaction pipeline
sections.summary: Using the SOFA physics simulator, the authors generate per-vertex contact force ground truth from hand-object collisions. The model consists of three stages: image feature extraction, iterative relative 3D pose refinement, and an estimation head conditioned on the refined pose to jointly predict contact and force.
sections.details:
Here is the full picture of EgoPHI and how its stages work:

### 3.1 Problem Formulation and Inputs
The model takes a monocular egocentric RGB image $\mathcal{I}$, left/right 3D hand vertex positions $\mathcal{P}_L, \mathcal{P}_R$, and an object template mesh $\mathcal{O}_{\text{template}}$. Off-the-shelf monocular estimators can provide hand poses, but because objects are heavily occluded, the network must jointly infer the object pose $(R, t)$ in camera space using visual and hand pose cues.

### 3.3 Contact and Force Supervision via Physics Simulation
To obtain dense 3D forces that are difficult to measure physically, the authors stream mesh animations from the ARCTIC interaction dataset into the SOFA physics simulator. Meshes are modeled as compliant bodies. When vertices penetrate the contact zone, a penalty method applies a restorative force $\mathbf{f}_i = k \cdot d_i \cdot \mathbf{n}_i$ proportional to penetration depth $d_i$, surface normal $\mathbf{n}_i$, and stiffness $k=10$. Applying a geometric contact mask $\mathcal{M}$ removes non-contact noise to yield clean per-vertex force vectors.

### 3.4 Data Representation
Directly regressing 3D force vectors leads to unstable training. EgoPHI decomposes the force into a scalar magnitude $|\mathbf{f}_i|$ and a unit direction vector $\mathbf{u}_i = \mathbf{f}_i / |\mathbf{f}_i|$. This stabilizes training and clarifies loss formulation.

### 3.5 Model Architecture (Three-Stage Pipeline)
- **Feature Extraction**: A ViT backbone extracts visual features, and mesh vertices are projected into the image using camera parameters to sample features via bilinear interpolation.
- **Iterative Pose Refinement**: Starting from an initial guess, the object pose is refined over $N=3$ iterations. The core Graph-Based Interaction Block blends Graph Attention Networks (GATs) along mesh topology with Cross-Attention between hands and objects, using hand positions to guide the object pose under occlusion.
- **Contact and Force Estimation**: Under the refined 3D object pose, a dedicated Interaction Block predicts per-vertex contact probabilities, force magnitudes, and force directions. Multiplying the predicted force by the contact probability ensures physical consistency by suppressing forces at non-contact points.

captions.F3: Physics-based force label generation. (a) A collision detection algorithm identifies hand-object proximity zones, and (b) generated forces are filtered with a contact mask to create physically plausible, noise-free ground-truth force distributions.

sections.heading: Backbone and training setup details
sections.summary: The model uses a ViT-B/16 visual backbone with 512-dimensional Interaction Blocks and three pose refinement iterations. Training uses ground-truth hand poses, while inference pairs the model with the state-of-the-art monocular hand pose estimator HAMER.
sections.details:
The backbone is ViT-B/16. The Interaction Blocks use an embedding dimension of $d=512$ with 4 attention heads. The Iterative Refinement Module (IRM) runs for 3 iterations.

During training, ground-truth hand poses from the dataset are provided. At test time, EgoPHI takes hand poses predicted from monocular RGB by HAMER. The model is trained using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of $1 \times 10^{-4}$ and a batch size of 8.

sections.heading: Rigorous evaluation across simulations, unseen benchmarks, and real-world sensing
sections.summary: EgoPHI significantly outperformed existing baselines on both in-distribution (ARCTIC) and out-of-distribution (H2O) datasets. An optical tactile sensing experiment further verified that the simulation-trained model reliably reconstructs contact and forces on real-world non-planar objects.
sections.details:
The experiments rested on two pillars: synthetic benchmark evaluations and real-world sim-to-real transfer.

### Baselines and Metrics
For 3D mesh evaluation, the authors fine-tuned HACO (a SOTA contact estimator) on their force labels, and compared against PressureVision in 2D image space. Force metrics include mean absolute error in contact regions (Masked MAE), root mean square error (Masked RMSE), and volumetric IoU (vIoU, evaluating spatial force distribution overlap).

### Benchmark Results (ARCTIC & H2O)
On ARCTIC (in-distribution), EgoPHI reduced force MAE and RMSE by roughly 2 N compared to HACO, alongside substantial vIoU gains. In 2D comparisons against PressureVision, it maintained robust localization despite hand occlusions. On the H2O dataset (out-of-distribution with unseen objects and environments), EgoPHI was the only method capable of estimating object contact and forces while demonstrating strong hand-force generalization.

### Ablation on Iterative Pose Refinement (IRM)
Compared to a baseline without pose refinement, IRM reduced vertex alignment error (MPV) by over 70% (from 64 cm down to 19 cm on ARCTIC), improving object force vIoU by up to a factor of three. Proper hand-object geometric alignment directly drives accurate force predictions.

### Real-World Sim-to-Real Validation
The authors fabricated acrylic sensing objects (a cuboid and a cylinder) exploiting frustrated total internal reflection (FTIR), where finger contact disrupts internal reflection and illuminates the skin. A bottom fisheye camera records brightness, converted into Newtons via a calibration lookup table built using a digital scale. Across ~2,000 synchronized frames from 8 participants, EgoPHI—trained purely on simulation—accurately captured contact regions and force intensities on novel real objects.

sections.heading: Remaining hurdles: temporal continuity, unknown shapes, and friction
sections.summary: While estimating 3D force fields from vision alone is now proven feasible, practical robotics adoption still faces hurdles: per-frame independent processing lacks temporal continuity, known template meshes are required, and only normal forces are modeled without tangential friction.
sections.details:
Despite impressive results, several limitations remain before full integration into practical robotics:

- **Unused Temporal Information**: Because EgoPHI processes frames independently, it lacks temporal dynamics and smooth continuity across time. Extending it to video sequences is needed.
- **Reliance on Prior 3D Meshes**: The approach assumes known 3D template meshes. For novel objects, it must be paired with monocular mesh reconstructors like SAM3D.
- **Normal-Only Force Estimation**: Current simulation and sensor setups capture only compressive normal forces perpendicular to surfaces, leaving out tangential frictional forces. Incorporating equations of motion and object accelerations via physics optimization is a promising next step.
- **Rigid Stiffness Assumption**: The simulation assigns a uniform stiffness to all objects, meaning the model cannot yet adapt to compliant, soft objects or objects with heterogeneous materials.

sections.heading: Moving from contact localization to true physical interaction reasoning
sections.summary: EgoPHI establishes a unified framework to jointly estimate dense 3D contact and forces on both hands and objects from egocentric RGB images. This work marks an essential step from superficial appearance recognition toward physically grounded interaction reasoning.
sections.details:
By combining visual features, 3D geometry, graph-based interaction reasoning, and iterative pose refinement, EgoPHI demonstrates that accurate 3D force distributions can be recovered from monocular cameras without wearable tactile sensors.

Showing a viable path for sim-to-real transfer—via physics simulation for label augmentation and FTIR sensing for real validation—is a major milestone. Reading how humans hold, apply force to, and manipulate objects from vision alone provides a vital foundation for robot imitation learning from human video demonstrations and safe physical human-robot collaboration.

takeaways: Explicitly modeling hand-object geometric interaction via graph blocks allows reasonable 3D contact force distribution estimation from monocular RGB without wearable tactile sensors.
Using a physics simulator (such as SOFA) on existing hand-object tracking datasets provides a highly scalable solution for generating difficult-to-measure dense 3D force ground truth.
Object pose errors severely degrade force estimation, making an iterative pose refinement module (IRM) guided by hand cues essential.
Acrylic sensing objects based on frustrated total internal reflection (FTIR) provide a practical, dense benchmark for evaluating sim-to-real transfer on non-planar surfaces.
limitations: Lacks temporal video modeling by processing frames independently, which leaves dynamic force changes and temporal consistency unaddressed.
Requires known 3D object template meshes in advance and cannot reconstruct unknown object geometry on the fly during force estimation.
Only predicts normal contact forces (pushing into surfaces), omitting tangential friction forces that govern grasp and manipulation stability.
Assumes a uniform stiffness parameter in simulation, meaning it cannot readily handle soft, deformable objects or items with variable material properties.
